subtitle: The everyday tool for comparing averages -- three flavors, one idea.

steps.label: t = DIFFERENCE / STANDARD ERROR
steps.sub: Big |t| = big difference relative to noise

steps.label: HEAVIER TAILS THAN NORMAL
steps.sub: Accounts for estimating spread from a small sample

code:
days = rng.normal(3.4, 1.0, 25).round(1)   # promised: 3.0-day delivery
t, p = stats.ttest_1samp(days, 3.0)
print(round(days.mean(),2), round(t,3), round(p,4))
# 3.38  2.055  0.0509
caption: Just above 0.05 -- doesn't mean "matches the promise," means this sample didn't quite clear it.

code:
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(desktop, mobile, equal_var=False)
print(desktop.mean() - mobile.mean())   # 7.91
print(round(t,3), round(p,4))           # 2.3  0.0246

# equal_var=True (Student's) on the SAME data: t=2.461, p=0.0155
caption: Welch's doesn't assume equal variances -- a safer default when groups clearly differ in spread.

eyebrow: How big is the gap? Cohen's d
code:
# mean difference in pooled standard deviations
d = 0.49   # medium effect
# rough labels: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large
caption: A p-value alone never tells you this -- always pair it with an effect size.

code:
before = rng.normal(80, 25, 20).round(2)
after = before + rng.normal(6, 12, 20)
t, p = stats.ttest_rel(after, before)
print(round(p, 4))   # 0.0011 -- a clear effect
caption: Analyzes the per-customer DIFFERENCE directly, removing customer-to-customer variation.

eyebrow: Analyzing it wrong: as two independent groups
code:
r = stats.ttest_ind(after, before, equal_var=False)
print(round(r.pvalue, 4))   # 0.2509 -- misses the SAME real effect
caption: Customer-to-customer spending differences drown the change -- pairing isn't a technicality.
